title: Node Irrigation in Beet Cultivation: Key Practical Tips
html:
Introduction to the Importance of Knot Irrigation in Sugar Beet Cultivation

Sugar beet, as one of the most important industrial crops in Iranian agriculture, requires precise management of water and soil resources. Traditional irrigation methods no longer meet the industry's growing demand for efficiency. In this context, Knot irrigation has emerged as a special role among the most advanced forms of drip irrigation. This method, by creating small and precise bursts of water at the plant's root zone, not only increases the uptake of water and nutrients but also prevents root rot and directly impacts the increase in root weight. In this article, we aim to examine the key points, benefits, and implementation principles of this system in a specialized manner, enabling farmers to benefit from it with confidence.

Main Advantages of the Knot Irrigation System for Sugar Beet

Why can choosing knot irrigation be a revolution in sugar beet farms? There are several reasons that make this system superior to the standard drip tape:

  • Reduced water stress: The knots inside the tape reduce the water flow velocity and increase irrigation precision, preventing the excessive wetting of the soil around the roots.
  • Improved water distribution: Water is delivered to the soil at lower pressure but with greater uniformity and more precise timing, which is essential for uniform beet root development.
  • Reduced water consumption: Practical comparisons have shown that the dripline system can reduce water consumption by 20-30 percent compared to surface irrigation.
  • Reduced weed growth: Since the soil surface between the rows remains dry, weed growth is significantly reduced.

Key considerations for selecting and installing drip tape

Choosing the correct product is half the success in irrigation. When purchasing drip tape for beet cultivation, special attention must be paid to the following technical specifications:

1. Selecting the appropriate wall thickness

Tape wall thickness directly affects system durability and resistance to dynamic and static pressure. For sugar beet, which requires high durability across varying climatic conditions, consulting with the guide for selecting the ideal tape wall thickness can be helpful. Typically, knot tapes with more robust walls are recommended for hot and dry climates.

2. Knot spacing and flow rate

Knot spacing must be adjusted based on climatic conditions, soil type, and the plant's growth stage. Sugar beet requires high-frequency, low-flow irrigation during the vegetative growth stage, but requires heavier, higher-flow irrigation during the bulb swelling stage. Using tapes with appropriate knots and either variable or standard fixed spacing guarantees uniform irrigation throughout the row. To better understand the design principles, review Key points for tape knot irrigation It is recommended.

3. Tuber row position

In beet cultivation, the drip line should be positioned exactly at the base of the plant (near the root zone). Any deviation of the line from the planting line will result in poor irrigation and yield reduction. Careful installation and the use of mechanized planting systems that install the drip line simultaneously with the seed are among the most important operational points.

Irrigation management and planning during different growth stages

Drip irrigation is not a passive system; it requires active management. Sugar beet has a specific growth cycle, and the irrigation schedule must be adjusted accordingly:

  1. Germination and emergence phase (Weeks 1-3): At this stage, the root system is weak and the plant is sensitive to water stress. Short, high-frequency irrigation (every 2-3 days) with low flow rates is recommended to prevent surface soil drying and crust formation.
  2. Rapid growth phase (Weeks 4-10): As leaf growth progresses and biomass volume begins to increase, irrigation demand peaks. At this stage, both the duration of irrigation and the outlet flow rate of the nozzles must be increased. Monitoring soil moisture at depths of 30-60 cm is essential.
  3. Tubercular bulking phase (Weeks 11-20): This is the most critical period for yield production. Irrigation should become deeper and less frequent to encourage roots to extend deeper into the soil profile. Abrupt cessation of irrigation or severe water stress will cause the tubers to harden and reduce sugar content.

For accurate calculation of irrigation requirements, understanding the water requirement per hectare is vital. Study the topic Bullock yield per hectare Although this relates to a different crop, the general principles for calculating the water efficiency factor and system pressure are applicable; the lower the desired pressure in the system, the more energy is saved in pump operation.

Practical tips to prevent nozzle clogging

Emitters are the nightmare of drip irrigation systems. To prevent this issue:

  • Advanced filtration: Using disc filters (120 micron or smaller) at the start of the system is essential. Any suspended particles, silt, or hard sediment can clog the emitters.
  • Dissolution: Given the nature of the crop, which requires specific biological processes, using pressurized irrigation to deliver appropriate biostimulants can optimize both watering and nutrient delivery.
  • Periodic cleaning: Before the start and end of each growing season, flush the system with citric acid or suitable cleaning agents to remove internal deposits.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Is the drip lateral system suitable for all soil types?

Yes, but its efficiency is higher in sandy and light soils with high permeability. In clay soils with low permeability, it may be necessary to reduce the flow rate of the drip emitters to prevent water from pooling on the surface. For specific climates, examining the differences in lateral drip technology inside and outside the country can help you consider more precise technical specifications.

What is the difference between drip lateral irrigation and standard drip irrigation?

The main difference lies in the water discharge mechanism. In standard drip lines, water exits through small orifices that are more sensitive to pressure variations. However, drip emitters create a hydrodynamic obstruction inside the tubing that causes water to be discharged at a more constant pressure and provides greater resistance to clogging. Therefore, drip lateral systems are a better option for farmers who prioritize quality and precision.
